items.title: The data already exists and is free
items.body: Sentinel-2 satellites photograph every parcel every 5 days at a 10-meter detail, at no cost. The raw material is available to everyone.

items.title: But only a few make use of it
items.body: Today only remote-sensing experts, with expensive software (ArcGIS, ENVI), turn those images into useful maps, and it takes them days or weeks. The field farmer is left out.

items2.title: Worldwide
items2.body: Agriculture is about 4% of world GDP and provides work to over 1.2 billion people (FAO).

items2.title: In Europe
items2.body: The Common Agricultural Policy (the European Union's main farming policy) is about 31% of the bloc's budget for 2021-2027.

items2.title: In Italy
items2.body: The agri-food sector is over 4% of national GDP and employs nearly 900,000 people (the ISTAT statistics institute).

slides.title: The questions an agronomist cannot answer alone
paras: These are the real questions the copilot answers in natural language, in under 10 seconds:
bullets: Which crop is in this parcel and what is its exact area in hectares?
How has the vegetation vigor (how green and healthy it is) evolved over the last 8 weeks?
Is there a sign of water shortage or anything unusual compared with previous years?
How does this parcel compare with its neighbors or with other regions of the country?
What growth stage is the crop in, and when is the best time to harvest?

cards.title: Informed decisions
cards.body: Insurers and governments refresh inventories monthly, not yearly: better subsidies, insurance and forecasting.

cards.title: New online service
cards.body: The copilot lets agronomists analyze how the crop grows through the year, by voice or text, with no experience in satellite imagery. Open Apache 2.0 license.

slides.title: Why segmentation is the key piece
slides.caption: Sentinel-2 input (RGB) · ground truth · TSViT-pheno prediction, pixel by pixel.
paras: Semantic segmentation labels every 10 × 10 meter pixel with the crop it belongs to. That is what makes it possible to:
bullets: Measure the exact area: with a mean overlap with the ground truth of 0.70 or more, the error drops below 1%.
Draw precise boundaries between different crops within the same parcel.
Detect problem spots (stress or pests) that a parcel-level analysis cannot see.
Validate against the official polygons of the farming administrations.

slides.title: CRISP-ML(Q) methodology
paras: The signal that separates crops lives in time, not in a single photo.

cells: Cost-benefit; we measure with the F1 score (balanced accuracy across crops); success = being able to tell 8 crops apart.
PASTIS-R + BreizhCrops; what counts is how the crop changes over the year; some crops have very few examples.
Vegetation indices, signals of the yearly change (Fourier transform and growth stages), AlphaEarth with 64 values, spatial cross-validation.
Simple models (random forest and XGBoost, a boosted decision tree) → detailed maps → model combinations → moving it to other areas.
Mean overlap with ground truth (mIoU) + detailed and grouped F1 score, how many crops to commit to, tests removing parts.
Servers that switch off on their own when idle + H100 card; copilot with live answers; data and experiment versioning.

slides.title: The data we use (all open)

cells: 64 values per pixel, 10 m, one summary per year (2017-2025). The main source.
18 crop types labeled by hand. Our main test bench.
Optical camera with 13 color bands, one image every 5 days.
Radar that sees through clouds (robust when the sky is overcast).
Extra land-use labels to validate in other regions.
28,482 agricultural questions and answers to evaluate the copilot.

paras: About 260 GB in total. Each source covers a weakness of the others.

items.label: labeled crops plus a background class

cards.title: Sentinel-2 optical series
cards.body: Between 38 and 61 dates per patch (mean ~48), from Sep-2018 to Nov-2019, with a 5 to 10-day revisit and 10 spectral bands. This is where the crop growth curve comes from.

cards.title: Sentinel-1 radar (the "R")
cards.body: About 70 radar observations per patch (ascending and descending orbits), in 3 channels (VV, VH and their ratio). Radar sees through clouds.

cards.title: Pixel-by-pixel labels
cards.body: Semantic segmentation (which crop is in each pixel) and panoptic (each parcel as an instance with its own id). Hand-annotated.

cards.title: Four regions of France
cards.body: Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, Grand Est, Hauts-de-France and Occitanie: four distinct agro-climatic zones, which forces the model to generalize.

slides.title: AlphaEarth Foundations (Google DeepMind)

items.label: values per pixel that summarize each place each year
detail per pixel · global coverage, including Mexico
one annual image per year (9 years available)

slides.sub2: Why it is our main source

cards.title: An already-digested summary
cards.body: DeepMind fuses optical, radar, Landsat, terrain and climate into 64 values per pixel. Instead of processing petabytes of imagery, we start from the ready-made summary.

cards.title: Stable across years
cards.body: For the same parcel, the 64 values barely change from one year to the next (about 95% similarity between consecutive years). That makes it reliable for comparison and for moving the model to new areas.

cards.title: Free and open
cards.body: CC-BY-4.0 license on Google Earth Engine: anyone can use it just by giving credit. No compute cost to generate it.

cards.title: Much information, little space
cards.body: In our project it takes up only about 6% of the total (~260 GB) and carries the highest density of useful information. It powers the simple model and is a member of the final ensemble.

slides.title: What matters is how the crop changes over the year
slides.caption: Map that groups similar parcels (UMAP) using AlphaEarth data.
bullets: The vegetation greenness index (NDVI) over the year separates crops; a single photo does not.
Summer maize versus winter cereals: they grow in different seasons → they are easy to tell apart.
Winter-cereal varieties that grow almost the same get confused, even with advanced neural networks.

slides.title: Severe class imbalance
slides.caption: Number of parcels per crop in PASTIS-R (18 classes).
bullets: Meadow alone is about 30 to 45% of parcels.
Rapeseed, sorghum, mixed cereal and potato: less than 1% each.
That is why we use the F1 score (which weighs every crop the same) and not the plain percentage of hits.

slides.title: Errors do not cluster geographically
bullets: The problem is in the crops that are hard to tell apart, not in areas with little data.
This means adding more data from a single region does not solve it.
We must make the crops easier to tell apart, not collect more samples.

items.title: Vegetation indices
items.body: Measures of plant greenness and moisture (NDVI, NDWI, EVI, MSAVI2, NDRE…).

items.title: Signals of the yearly change
items.body: Growth rhythms with the Fourier transform; plant stages: when it greens up, its peak and when it dries out.

items.title: The 64 AlphaEarth values
items.body: Yeo-Johnson adjustments to fix skewed values.

slides.title: Spatial cross-validation — without letting the model cheat
slides.caption: The map is split into blocks; the test blocks (lighter) are set apart from the training ones, with a gap between them.
bullets: We split the map into zones (with H3 cells and clustering) and leave a 1 km gap between training and test zones.
We go from each pixel up to each whole parcel.
The system stops on its own if it finds those zones overlapping.

slides.title: Why do we use the F1 score?

items.title: The percentage of hits misleads
items.body: When one crop dominates, always saying that crop gives a high but misleading percentage of hits.

items.title: The F1 score treats all crops equally
items.body: Rare and common crops count the same → aligned with the business. Rapeseed insurance matters even if rapeseed is just 1%.

slides.title: Key segmentation takeaway
slides.caption: Scores of the 6 architectures (overlap with ground truth and F1 score).
bullets: It confirms that what tells crops apart is how they change over time, not their texture.
paras: Models that watch the change over the year (TSViT, U-TAE) beat by far those that only look at the shape in the image.

slides.title: TSViT, in simple words
slides.caption: Each crop has a typical greenness pattern across the year: it sprouts, grows, ripens. The model learns that curve.
bullets: It is a model that analyzes separately how each area changes over time and how it looks in the image.
Its TSViT-pheno version compares each pixel with the typical growth pattern of each crop.
It takes the average greenness curve, asks Gemini for a description and turns it into numbers. Method by Wen and colleagues, 2025.

bullets: Winter barley 0.89 · soft winter wheat 0.86 · grapevine 0.86 · meadow 0.81.
Mixed cereal 0.24 (the worst).
Takeaway: crops with a clear yearly growth and many examples win.

slides.kicker: The model we take to production
slides.title: The winner: twelve well-resolved crops

cards.title: Why twelve and not eighteen
cards.body: By focusing on the twelve crops the system separates clearly, accuracy rises from 0.79 to 0.90 without losing the bulk of business value: those twelve cover 90% of parcels. The remaining six are rare, lookalike crops better reviewed by hand.

cards.title: It improves with each new region
cards.body: This model is not static: it is refreshed with data from new regions through transfer learning. Adding Lower Saxony (Germany) lifted winter cereals (wheat, maize, rye, rapeseed) from a low score to between 0.57 and 0.70. Each new region makes it more robust.

slides.title: The copilot that converses
paras: The models see the crops; a language model reasons and answers.

slides.title: Be My Eyes pattern: one sees, the other reasons

items.title: The models SEE (the perceiver)
items.body: The vision models look at the satellite imagery and describe it in plain text: which crop it is, its growth stage, how vigorous it looks and how much confidence there is. They don't decide: they just report what they see, and the answer always says which model looked (the Voting-3 winner or, outside its universe, XGBoost).

items.title: The language model REASONS
items.body: Gemini or Qwen take that description, query the 10 map tools and answer the agronomist's question in natural language. Like a guide who describes what the camera sees to someone who cannot see it.

slides.title: Three language models to choose from — control of the data

items.title: Gemini 3.5 Flash (in the cloud)
items.body: Generally available, can read very long texts and answers fast. It is the brain that reasons by default in the copilot.

items.title: Qwen 3.5 MoE (on our own server)
items.body: Runs on our own graphics card: the data never leaves home. A language model to reason without depending on the cloud.

items.title: Qwen 3.6 VL (on our own server)
items.body: A model that also sees images (vision-language). You switch between the three with a toggle, without touching the code.

slides.kicker: The toggle works · same question, same eyes
slides.title: Three brains, the same answer
slides.sub2: Real question: "What crop is in parcel 52?"

cards.title: All three agree
cards.body: With the same fixed perceiver, all three models answer the same: soft winter wheat, 97.9% confidence. What changes is the response time, not the result: switching between cloud and our own server is transparent to the agronomist.

slides.title: The 10 map tools

cells: Lists the parcels inside an area
Gives the real key dates of the growth
Searches images in the Copernicus data service
Classifies a parcel with the Voting-3 winner (F1 0.90, 12 crops)

paras: All are real, they check that the input data is valid and only access each user's own session data.

slides.kicker: How the agent answers, step by step
slides.title: It acts on real data first, then writes

items.title: 1 · Plans
items.body: Given the agronomist's question, the agent decides which tools it needs (for example, list the parcels and explain their prediction).

items.title: 2 · Calls the tool
items.body: It runs those tools on the session's real database: no made-up data. Every call is logged.

items.title: 3 · Gets the result
items.body: The tool returns real figures (crop, confidence, dates, hectares) that the agent can cite.

items.title: 4 · Writes and cites
items.body: Only then it writes the answer in natural language, with each figure tied to its source. If something is missing, it says so.

slides.kicker: So it does not make up data
slides.title: Search with geographic context (Spatial-RAG)

items.title: 1. Filter by closeness
items.body: PostGIS (ST_DWithin) keeps only the parcels that are near the queried area. The "where" first.

items.title: 2. Rank by similarity
items.body: Among those nearby parcels, pgvector finds the most similar to the question (similarity over the embeddings) and returns the best ones. Then the "what".

items.title: 3. Answer on real grounding
items.body: The language model reasons only over those real parcels from the session, not over what it thinks it knows. That way it reduces hallucinations.

slides.title: Security
slides.caption: Layered defense: from the user session to controlled sources.
bullets: Each user only reaches their own session data (row-level security, no exceptions).
The tools are limited and out-of-range inputs are rejected.
Everything is logged and can be reviewed.
Malicious messages → the tools are limited.
Poisoned information in the search → we use only controlled sources.
Over-confidence → it warns when confidence is below 0.60.

slides.title: An honest app
paras: When information is missing it says so clearly, instead of making up data:
bullets: Time series: it only shows the real measured dates.
Image search: it shows up empty if that catalog is not available yet.
Background tasks: it explicitly states they are not implemented yet.

slides.title: Does it extend to other regions?
paras: Transfer learning, good practices and lessons learned.

slides.kicker: The bar we set ourselves, and the honesty of missing it
slides.title: We wanted to repeat France's 0.90 in another region
paras: The ambitious goal was clear: take the model trained in France (F1 score of 0.90 on 12 crops) to a new region and reach that 0.90 again with the same recipe, without retraining from scratch.
bullets: Measuring it with real data required two datasets that did not exist: we built them ourselves (Italy and Germany).
Honest spoiler: in Italy we did NOT reach it (ceiling 0.12) and in Germany we got close (8 crops above 0.60), but France's 0.90 is not yet reached in a new region.
The limit is not the number of regions, but that many crops don't separate well from only the yearly image summary.

slides.kicker: Step 1 · Build the data to be able to measure
slides.title: We built our own PASTIS-style datasets

items.label: new datasets built by hand (Italy 2018 and Germany 2023), not downloaded

slides.sub2: The methodology, step by step (they did not exist in PASTIS format: building them is what lets us measure transfer)

cards.title: 1 · Official labels
cards.body: We start from parcel polygons with their declared crop, from public European agricultural registries (EuroCrops): Tuscany 2018 and Lower Saxony 2023.

cards.title: 2 · PASTIS-style patches
cards.body: The area is split into 128 × 128 pixel patches with the full Sentinel-2 image series of the period (24 dates in Italy, ~41 in Germany) and a pixel-wise mask with each parcel's crop: the same format as the French dataset.

cards.title: 3 · Summaries and clean splits
cards.body: Each parcel gets its AlphaEarth summary (via Google Earth Engine) and the area is split into 5 geographic blocks, so evaluation happens on areas the model has never seen.

slides.kicker: Step 2 · The results on our own datasets
slides.title: Does it work in other regions?

items.title: Italy (Tuscany) — hard
items.body: Very small parcels (0.4 ha) and only 8 months observed: on the full dataset (103,350 parcels) the model barely reaches an F1 score of 0.12. Except grapevine (0.64), Mediterranean crops get confused.

items.title: Germany (Lower Saxony) — it works
items.body: Large parcels (10 ha) and 14 months observed: the F1 score rises to 0.266 (2.2× more than Tuscany). Cereals are rescued: maize 0.70, rapeseed 0.69, wheat 0.67, rye 0.57.

slides.kicker: Not even within the same country is it automatic
slides.title: France → Brittany: the region already changes the result
slides.caption: Tabular classifier trained in France (PASTIS 2019, the 185 shared features) and evaluated directly on Brittany (public BreizhCrops 2017 dataset, 2,145 parcels), without retraining. Since BreizhCrops has no AlphaEarth, this test uses the tabular model over the 7 shared crops, not Voting-3.
bullets: Brittany is France, but it is another region: Atlantic climate, different calendar, different year, different parcels.
Even so, taking the classifier directly is not automatic: overall F1 score of only 0.21.
It holds where the crop looks the same: rapeseed 0.70, meadow 0.51. It collapses on cereals: maize 0.14, barley 0.07, wheat 0.01.
The lesson that guides the whole chapter: changing region is a real jump, not just changing country.

slides.title: Italy: we tried transfer 3 ways
slides.caption: Same model (TSViT-pheno) and same metric over the 39 Italian classes (test fold-3). How much each way of transferring adds.
bullets: Training from scratch, only with Italian data: F1 score 0.095.
Pure transfer: reuse what the model already learned in France about reading the image series, with a new classifier for the Italian crops: 0.120.
Keeping the classes: also starting the classifier from the French crops, or replicating the PASTIS training mode: 0.130–0.132.
What helps most is what it learned about reading the images; keeping the French classes adds little on average.

slides.title: Does keeping France's classes help?
slides.caption: F1-score difference per kept crop: how much it changes when starting from the French model instead of at random.
bullets: On average keeping the classes helps a bit (+0.012), but it is not universal.
It helps where the crop looks alike France-Italy: durum wheat +0.08, barley +0.07, alfalfa +0.05.
It hurts where it differs: oats −0.08, sunflower −0.06, soft wheat −0.04 (different Mediterranean phenology).
Honest finding: France's knowledge transfers crop by crop, not as a block.

slides.kicker: The region where moving the model to a new area DOES work — 3 measured factors
slides.title: Germany (Lower Saxony): why it works

cells: More usable dates (24 → 56 in Tuscany; ~41 in Germany): rescues cereals

slides.title: DE4 — rescued cereals
slides.caption: F1 score per crop of Voting-3 in Germany DE4 (53,460 parcels). In green, the cereals that were sunk in Tuscany.
bullets: Maize 0.70 · rapeseed 0.69 · grassland 0.68 · winter wheat 0.67 · rye 0.57.
8 crops scoring 0.6 or more, against just 1 in Tuscany.
The 3 evaluation ways agree: keeping the area's classes 0.266 · translating them to a common list 0.287 · full procedure 0.266.
Large parcels (10 ha versus 0.4) + full year + watching the winter = crops are easier to tell apart.

slides.kicker: Step 3 · Now we validate the idea on other teams' public data
slides.title: Three supporting studies on public datasets

items.title: So we don't depend only on our data
items.body: So far we tested transfer with our datasets (Italy, Germany). Now we repeat the same idea on three third-party public datasets. All three confirm the lesson: changing region is a real jump and local examples are needed.

items.title: France → Catalonia (Sen4AgriNet)
items.body: With the public Sen4AgriNet dataset of Catalan parcels: with no local examples the French model gets nothing right (0.00); with a few examples per crop it reaches 0.25.

items.title: Latvia → Estonia (EuroCropsML)
items.body: With the public EuroCropsML dataset of Baltic parcels: when moving from one country to another, AlphaEarth summaries beat raw Sentinel-2 imagery with any number of examples (+0.111 with a single example per crop).

items.title: Europe → Brazil (WorldCereal)
items.body: With ESA WorldCereal public labels in the Brazilian Cerrado (only maize also exists in Europe): with no examples 0.01; with 20 examples per crop 0.63. The tropics need local examples.

slides.kicker: Zooming into the 2nd study: Latvia → Estonia
slides.title: Why we use AlphaEarth and not raw imagery
slides.caption: Latvia → Estonia (EuroCropsML): F1 score on Estonia by number of examples per crop, mean of 3 seeds.
bullets: The previous Latvia → Estonia study, in detail: we compare two ways of describing each parcel.
Google's AlphaEarth summaries vs raw Sentinel-2 imagery: with a single example per crop, AlphaEarth scores 0.43 and raw scores 0.32 (+0.111).
The edge holds with few examples (+0.087 at 5) and both converge once saturated.
Takeaway: AlphaEarth brings useful knowledge out of the box and reaches the same level with ~10 times fewer labels — key for new regions where labeling is expensive.

slides.kicker: Another strategy: one single model for several regions
slides.title: Training with several regions at once improves many crops
slides.caption: F1-score difference per crop: multi-region model (30 crops) minus the France-only one (18), on the same test and budget.
bullets: Instead of transferring the French model, we tried training one single classifier with several European regions together: the list grows from 18 to 30 crops.
Adding regions does improve many crops: potato +0.64, spring barley +0.38, grassland +0.28, winter soft wheat +0.28.
Only 2 of 30 get slightly worse (sunflower −0.11): the balance is clearly positive.
Looking only at a threshold (how many cross 0.85?) was hiding these real per-crop gains.

slides.title: A negative result we report honestly
paras: With that multi-region strategy the crop list DOES grow (from 18 to 30, without forcing equivalences) and the per-crop balance is positive, but:

No NEW crop (exclusive to other regions) crosses an F1 score of 0.85: the 2 that do were already learnable in France. The bottleneck is that many crops don't separate well from only the yearly summary, not the number of regions.
bullets: Multi-region (30 crops): 7 above 0.70, 2 above 0.85.
France only (18, same budget): 6 above 0.70, 2 above 0.85.
New crops rescued above 0.85: 0.
Overall multi-region F1 score 0.65, on par with the single-region baseline (0.6535), despite predicting 30 crops instead of 18.

slides.title: How we organize work with AI assistants

items.title: Assistant organization
items.body: A single central guide, 30 specialized skills, 9 expert assistants, per-folder guides loaded when needed and a memory that persists across sessions.

items.title: Best practices
items.body: English code and Spanish text, no emojis, tidy logs, declared types, no repeated code, separated responsibilities, several isolated clients, several languages, passwords in a secure manager, versioned data and controlled database changes.

slides.title: Rigor: how we avoided fooling ourselves
paras: The decisions that keep the numbers credible, not inflated:
bullets: Spatial cross-validation: training and test in separate zones (1 km buffer), so the model can't memorize neighbors and the numbers are real.
Zero filler data: everything you see came from real data; when something was missing, the system says so rather than making it up.
Honest metric: we report balanced accuracy and its coverage, not just the nicest-looking number.
Verifiable reproducibility: notebooks run from start to finish with results visible, quality and security checks, and over 70% of the server code covered by tests.

slides.title: Lessons learned
paras: Five things we learned along the way, each backed by an experiment in the project:
bullets: Time matters more than shape: how the crop changes over the year tells crops apart better than its appearance in a single image (that's why the winner is a temporal model, TSViT-pheno).

Changing region is a real jump: taking the model to a new area drops it hard (Tuscany 0.12, Brittany 0.21). It works where the crop looks alike and parcels are large (Germany), and needs local examples in every new zone.
Google's base models (AlphaEarth) pay off: they reach the same accuracy with ~10 times fewer labels, but they do no magic with no local examples at all.
Simple can win: combining 3 models with a simple vote was as accurate and more reliable than a 5-model ensemble with 54 internal settings (Voting-3 vs Stacking-5).
Honesty is part of the contribution: also reporting what did not work across regions leaves the real limit on the record, not hidden.

slides.sub2: The message that ties the whole talk together

cards.title: It solves the real problem
cards.body: It turns free satellite imagery into answers an agronomist understands, in seconds and in natural language. The copilot sees with the models and reasons with an LLM (Be My Eyes pattern), always citing its source.

cards.title: It is honest about its limits
cards.body: It also reports what did not work: taking the model to a new region is a real jump. When it doesn't know, it says so; it never makes things up. That transparency is part of the contribution.

cards.title: It reproduces end to end
cards.body: Versioned data and experiments (DVC · MLflow · Dagster), infrastructure as code and notebooks run with their results visible. Anyone can repeat it.
